Finding: JWT is required globally in the contract, but the contract cannot verify signature, issuer, audience, expiry, or algorithm. The Prism mock accepted the placeholder 'Bearer test-token'. A forged or unsigned token would pass if middleware validation is missing or misconfigured.
Mitigation: Validate every JWT in Express middleware using the Entra JWKS endpoint: verify RS256 signature, reject alg=none, check iss and aud, reject expired tokens. Return 401 on failure. Keep /health on an allow-list.

Finding: ID-based endpoints (for example GET /books/{bookId}/loans) document the ownership rule in prose but the contract cannot enforce it. A query filtering only by resource ID lets any member read another member's loan history (BOLA). Building scoping does not fix this within the same building.
Mitigation: Enforce ownership in the query itself for every /{id} endpoint, using both a building predicate and an owner/recipient predicate in the WHERE clause. Derive caller identity from the validated JWT. Return 404 for the not-owner case on privacy-sensitive reads. Verify with BOLA tests.

Finding: The design intends parameterised access, but two common concatenation spots exist: the LIKE pattern on free-text search (GET /books?search=...) and any dynamic WHERE/ORDER BY built from filter and sort parameters. No concatenated query was found; this is a control to preserve.
Mitigation: Use parameterised queries for every value. Keep search text as a bound parameter with only wildcards in the query. Never concatenate a column name for ORDER BY; validate the sort field against a fixed allow-list. Enforce in code review and static-analysis linting.

Finding: Secrets are mandated to Azure Key Vault by constraint. Residual risks: a bootstrap secret used to reach Key Vault, a developer .env committed by accident, secrets printed in CI logs, connection strings captured in telemetry, and missing rotation.
Mitigation: Store all connection strings and keys in Key Vault; read them at startup via a Managed Identity so no bootstrap secret exists. Keep secrets out of source control and mask them in CI logs. Add secrets to the telemetry redaction list. Rotate at least quarterly and immediately on suspected exposure.

Finding: TLS is part of the design (Front Door terminates TLS; SQL, Redis, and Service Bus are over TLS). Residual risks: plain HTTP may be redirected rather than rejected, exposing the first authenticated request, and the Front Door to App Service hop may be unencrypted.
Mitigation: Enforce HTTPS-only at Front Door and reject plain HTTP; send the HSTS header. Enable HTTPS on the origin so the Front Door to App Service hop is encrypted, and set App Service to HTTPS Only. Keep backend connections on TLS 1.2 or higher.

Finding: Front Door rate limiting exists (runbook: ~100/min per IP general, 20/min per member writes), but the 5/min login limit targets an endpoint this API does not expose (Entra owns login), and sensitive ID-based read endpoints are only bounded by the loose general 100/min bucket, leaving enumeration weakly limited.
Mitigation: Add a stricter per-member limit on write endpoints. Add a tighter limit on ID-based read endpoints, well below the general bucket, to slow enumeration. Rate-limit repeated 401/403 responses per IP and log them. Return 429 with Retry-After.

Finding: Responses and queue messages are ID-only by design, which is good. Residual risk is in logs and telemetry: audit logs hold member IDs by requirement (no access-control or retention rule stated), error logging can capture request bodies, App Insights can capture SQL parameter values, and the digest worker could log member email addresses.
Mitigation: Keep responses and queues ID-only. Define a redaction list (email, address, phone, tokens, connection strings, full bodies) applied before logging. Log the member ID in the digest worker, never the email. Configure App Insights to record query shape without parameter values. Restrict audit-log access to security/ops and set a retention period.

Finding: OWASP ZAP baseline scan found the response header Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * (wildcard CORS). This is the Prism mock's default, not configured by the spec, so it is a false positive against the design, but a wildcard CORS policy on the deployed API (which serves private member data) would let any website attempt cross-origin reads.
Mitigation: Restrict Access-Control-Allow-Origin in production to the known BookSwap front-end origin instead of a wildcard. Re-verify with an active ZAP scan once a real backend exists.

Finding: OWASP ZAP baseline scan flagged responses without explicit cache-control headers (Storable and Cacheable Content). Raised only on empty 404 pages on the mock (false positive here), but private production responses such as loan history could be retained by a shared cache if no-store is not set.
Mitigation: Send Cache-Control: no-store on private responses (loan history, borrow requests, notifications) so no proxy or shared cache retains member data.
